recall.a: Deontology: follow the rules (don't break promises, steal, etc.) regardless of outcome. Consequentialism/utilitarianism: judge by outcomes, maximise utility; act vs rule variants differ in whether each act or the general rule is judged.
recall.q: Contrast deontology and utilitarianism in one breath.

recall.a: Deontology says don't pull (killing violates the rule); act-utilitarianism may permit it (one death vs five). The point is that reasonable frameworks disagree — ethics needs deliberation, not slogans.
recall.q: What do the two frameworks say about the trolley, and what is the lesson?

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Ethics is personal, cultural, ideological — about how human beings, not just software, can come to harm. The unit opens the topic with moral philosophy because software engineers hold power over people they will never meet, and power without a framework for right and wrong is just luck. The midterm tests this as reasoning, not recitation: Worksheet 5 asks for stories, not slogans.

sections.heading: Two schools of thought

head: School
Right action is...
Example reasoning
rows: Adherence to rules: don't break promises, steal, harm — whatever the payoff
Don't falsify test results even if shipping late costs the contract
Whatever maximises utility (happiness, welfare); act judges each act, rule judges the general rule
Pull the trolley lever: one death instead of five (act-utilitarian)

paras: The handout's map (Figure 1) splits consequentialism into utilitarianism, then rule vs act utilitarianism, set against deontology's rule list. Utilitarianism answers deontology's rigidity — rules collide, and strict obedience can mandate cruelty — provided you can define and measure 'utility', which is itself contested. Neither school wins; the unit's point is that you can now name the disagreement instead of waving at it.

sections.heading: The trolley problem
paras: An out-of-control tram will kill five people tied to the tracks; you can pull a lever to divert it, killing one person instead. Deontology recoils (do not kill, full stop); act-utilitarianism calculates (one is fewer than five). The lecture uses it to show that moral principles and their practical integration differ — knowing the theory does not dissolve the dilemma, it structures your deliberation about it. In software terms: every 'move fast' shortcut is a small trolley decision about other people's safety, privacy and livelihoods.

summary: Moral philosophy gives engineers two lenses — duty to rules vs outcomes for the many — whose honest disagreement (see: trolley) is the start of ethical deliberation.
title: Moral philosophy: duties vs consequences

activities.prompt: Match each claim to its school

left.label: 'Pull the lever: one death beats five'

activities.explanation: Duty judges the act; utility judges the outcome. The frameworks can honestly disagree — which is why engineers must deliberate explicitly.

activities.prompt: Scenario: the client leans on your estimates
activities.instructions: You and two colleagues are mid-planning-poker. The client says the bid must come down or the contract walks. Decide.

pressure.text: Estimates say 40 days; the client demands 25 and hints the contract depends on it. The team looks at you. What do you do?

options.label: Trim the cards to 25 to keep the contract
options.note: Knowingly false estimates betray the team and future users.

options.label: Refuse to change the numbers, disclose the uncertainty and offer options
options.note: Honesty plus options: the ACS stakeholder-trust response.

options.label: Say nothing and let the loudest voice decide
options.note: Silence delegates your professional judgement to pressure.

falsified.text: The project 'commits' to 25 days, overruns to 43, and the client you tried to please terminates anyway. The team absorbs unpaid overtime.
falsified.title: Numbers bent
falsified.debrief: Falsified estimates help nobody: the overrun still arrives, now compounded by broken trust. Public and stakeholder interest outranks client pressure in the ACS Code.

silent.text: Estimates drift down under pressure. Nobody owns the numbers, so nobody defends them — the same overrun, with deniability instead of integrity.
silent.title: Diffusion
silent.debrief: Diffusion of responsibility is how groups misbehave. Professionalism means owning your estimate out loud, even when it costs.

honest.text: You hold the 40-day estimate, show the breakdown, and offer scope phasing: core in 25 days, remainder next. The client pushes back. Now what?

options.label: Offer the phased scope in writing with risks stated
Concede the 40 was 'pessimistic' to smooth things over
options.note: Same falsification, slower — and now documented as yours.

phased.text: The client accepts phased delivery. The team ships the core on time; trust — the currency the ACS Code protects — survives the negotiation.
phased.title: Held the line
phased.debrief: Duty (don't lie) plus utility (a shippable core) plus code (stakeholder trust first). Frameworks converge here: honesty with options.

activities.explanation: Estimate pressure is the handout's own scenario (Example 4). The pattern generalises: disclose, document, offer options — never silently comply.

visuals.caption: Deontology judges the act (do not kill); act-utilitarianism judges the outcome (one death vs five). The unit's lesson: name the framework, show the reasoning.
